cards.front: Chorioretinitis, microcephaly or hydrocephalus, convulsions and intracranial calcification form the classical neonatal tetrad of congenital [___].
cards.context:
The tetrad is how this infection shows itself in a newborn: eye, head growth, seizures and intracranial calcification. One feature on its own does not name it.

This is Sabin's tetrad. The RCH handbook quotes a triad: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcification. A blueberry-muffin rash may also occur.

Raw or undercooked meat and cat faeces are the transmission routes. The mother may have been asymptomatic.

cards.front: The hypothalamus must release GnRH in [___] to keep LH and FSH secretion going.
cards.context:
The pituitary only answers GnRH that arrives in bursts. A steady GnRH signal desensitises its receptors, so LH and FSH fall after a brief flare.

That is why a long-acting GnRH agonist is used to switch the ovaries off in endometriosis and some cancers.

cards.front: At 28 weeks, a woman has immune anti-D and a D-positive fetus that has never been transfused. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is 1.7 multiples of the gestational median (median 1.0). This finding raises concern for fetal [___].
cards.context:
Anaemia lowers viscosity and increases cerebral flow velocity. The peak systolic velocity is interpreted against gestational age.

This is different from the reduced cerebral vascular resistance of brain sparing in placental insufficiency.

cards.front: On day 9 after a vaginal birth, a woman has fresh bleeding of about 600 mL, offensive lochia, a temperature of 38.4 °C and a tender, bulky uterus. By timing, this is a [___] postpartum haemorrhage.
cards.context:
NSW Health defines primary PPH as 500 mL or more within 24 hours of birth, and secondary PPH as 500 mL or more from 24 hours to 6 weeks.

Secondary PPH usually follows endometritis or retained products. Look for infection, and image when retained products are suspected.

cards.front: Labour requires three components: regular painful contractions with progressive cervical [___] and dilatation.
cards.context:
The diagnostic criteria for labour are deliberately strict: REGULAR (timed, recurring), PAINFUL contractions with PROGRESSIVE cervical change.

Braxton-Hicks contractions are irregular and usually painless, without progressive cervical change. Latent-phase contractions may be painful and irregular.

Painful contractions without demonstrated cervical change need assessment and sometimes reassessment. They may represent early labour or false labour; discharge depends on maternal and fetal wellbeing.

cards.front: Preconception planning should begin [___] months before conception; the five pillars include folate, lifestyle, medication review, chronic disease control, and reproductive carrier screening.
cards.context:
The 3-6 month window matters because highest-risk fetal development precedes a recognised pregnancy. The neural tube closes by day 28 and organogenesis is done by 12 weeks, so optimisation must precede conception.

Five pillars: folate; lifestyle (smoking, alcohol, weight); medication review (switch teratogens: warfarin, ACEi/ARB, methotrexate, isotretinoin); carrier screening (identify carrier couples early).

Plus chronic disease control: diabetes, epilepsy, SLE and thyroid stable BEFORE conception, when first-trimester glycaemia and disease activity set anomaly and miscarriage risk.

cards.front: Pre-eclampsia diagnosis requires hypertension after 20 weeks PLUS new [___] involvement (renal, hepatic, haematological, neurological, pulmonary, or placental).
cards.context:
2018 ISSHP/SOMANZ broadened pre-eclampsia from 'HTN + proteinuria' to 'HTN + ANY new organ involvement' — ~20% of pre-eclampsia has no significant proteinuria but still has organ dysfunction.

Every visit after 20 weeks checks blood pressure, symptoms and urine protein. Creatinine, LFTs and FBC follow when hypertension or symptoms appear.

cards.front: If labour is established and birth is unlikely by 18 hours after membrane rupture, start intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis at [___].
cards.context:
Eighteen hours of rupture is the risk threshold. Waiting until that hour can leave no antibiotic running before the baby is born.

When labour is already established and birth will not occur by 18 hours, the start time is 14 hours after rupture.

cards.front: Secondary PPH (24 hours to 6 weeks postpartum) is most commonly due to [___] or endometritis; investigate with pelvic ultrasound.
cards.context:
Retained placental tissue and endometritis (infection of the uterine lining) can prevent normal uterine involution, causing bleeding 24 hours to 6 weeks after birth.

Fever, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia support endometritis. Assess blood loss and haemodynamic status first; check a full blood count.

Pelvic ultrasound helps assess retained tissue, but normal postpartum appearances can be misleading. If infection is suspected, take indicated cultures and start broad-spectrum antibiotics without waiting for results.

cards.front: Chorionicity must be determined by ultrasound (USS) at 11–14 weeks. lambda sign = dichorionic; [___] = monochorionic.
cards.context:
Chorionicity means placental sharing, and it drives twin-pregnancy risk more than zygosity. It is best assigned on first-trimester ultrasound scan (USS), before the inter-twin membrane becomes harder to interpret.

Lambda/twin-peak sign means dichorionic twins with placental tissue between membranes. T sign means monochorionic twins, who need closer surveillance for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

cards.front: A woman with previous gestational diabetes and BMI 36 has a normal 75 g OGTT at 12 weeks. She should have the test repeated at [___] weeks.
cards.context:
Women with risk factors, such as previous gestational diabetes or obesity, are tested early in pregnancy.

A normal early result does not exclude later insulin resistance, so the test is repeated in the usual window.

cards.front: Ovarian torsion: sudden unilateral pain + adnexal mass; normal Doppler flow does NOT exclude it, because the ovary has a dual blood supply; requires emergency [___] for ovarian salvage.
cards.context:
Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency — twisting of ovary on its pedicle → ischaemia/necrosis.

Doppler trap: dual blood supply (ovarian artery + uterine artery via ovarian branch) — partial torsion can show preserved Doppler flow despite ischaemia.

Prompt laparoscopy and detorsion offer the best chance of salvage. There is no established time cutoff for irreversible damage; delayed presentation does not justify abandoning ovarian preservation.

cards.front: Abundant lanugo on a newborn is a sign of [___].
cards.context:
Lanugo covers the fetus in mid-pregnancy and is mostly shed before term.

Plenty of it on a newborn points to a baby born early, and it is one of the physical signs scored when gestation is estimated.

cards.front: The ideal fetal presentation is flexed vertex, occiput [___]; the smallest presenting diameter is the suboccipitobregmatic (~9.5 cm).
cards.context:
Full flexion presents the suboccipitobregmatic diameter, about 9.5 cm. Occiput anterior describes the direction of the occiput; flexion describes the head's attitude.

Deflexed vertex presents a larger diameter; persistent brow is particularly obstructive. Fully extended face presents the submentobregmatic diameter, also about 9.5 cm.

Occiput posterior often accompanies deflexion and can prolong labour. Face presentation is not automatically too wide: chin position and labour progress determine whether vaginal birth is possible.

cards.front: From 14 weeks, women who cannot access NIPT are told that the publicly funded option is [___].
cards.context:
NIPT is more accurate after the first trimester, but it has no Medicare rebate. Women who cannot pay or travel still need a screen they can reach.

Second trimester serum screening is that publicly funded option. It may be considered when no earlier screen has been done.

cards.front: In Australia, miscarriage means pregnancy loss before 20 weeks; the most common cause of early miscarriage is fetal [___].
cards.context:
Pooled international data estimate miscarriage in about 15% of recognised pregnancies; this is not an Australian registry estimate. Chromosomal abnormalities cause many early miscarriages.

Further assessment depends on timing, recurrence and clinical findings. Birth-registration rules are separate from this clinical definition.

reference.title: Miscarriage, Recurrent Miscarriage and Ectopic Pregnancy (C-Gyn 38)

cards.front: Prolapse treatment follows symptom burden, not POP-Q stage: the main non-surgical treatments are pelvic floor muscle training and a vaginal [___], with surgery if these fail or are declined.
cards.context:
Pelvic organ prolapse is graded by the position of the leading edge relative to the hymen (POP-Q stages 0-IV).

The trap is treating the stage rather than the patient — many women with stage II prolapse (descent within 1 cm of the hymen) are completely asymptomatic.

cards.front: Decelerations that mirror contractions and are caused by fetal head compression are [___] decelerations.
cards.context:
Early decelerations slow gradually as the contraction develops and return to baseline by its end. Compare the fetal heart-rate and contraction traces together to recognise this timing pattern.

The label alone does not establish fetal wellbeing. Assess the baseline, variability, other trace features and the maternal and fetal clinical picture; seek senior review when there are concerning changes.

cards.front: Australian guidance says information on reproductive genetic carrier screening should be offered to [___] women planning a pregnancy or in early pregnancy, not only those with a family history.
cards.context:
The test is offered, then it waits. It goes ahead only when the woman's values and preferences are accepted.

Declining is a complete decision. It is not a cue to insist, and it is not a missed screen.

cards.front: A complete hydatidiform mole is most often karyotype 46,XX with entirely paternal genetic origin. No fetal tissue is present; malignant risk is [___]%.
cards.context:
Complete mole: empty ovum fertilised by sperm that duplicates its DNA; most are 46,XX and entirely paternal, with no fetal tissue.

Compared with partial mole, complete mole has higher βhCG and malignant risk. Manage with suction curette, then βhCG surveillance; plateau or rise means persistent GTN.

cards.front: A woman has thin grey vaginal discharge, a fishy odour and clue cells. Her vaginal flora has shifted towards anaerobes, with loss of the normally dominant genus [___].
cards.context:
Lactobacilli produce lactic acid, maintaining an acidic vaginal environment. Their depletion permits anaerobic overgrowth and the characteristic discharge and odour.

Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells coated with bacteria; they support bacterial vaginosis rather than candidiasis.

cards.front: [___] syndrome is a severe pre-eclampsia variant defined by a microangiopathic blood-film picture, raised transaminases, and thrombocytopenia.
cards.context:
About 15% of HELLP occurs without hypertension or proteinuria, so diagnosis rests on the lab triad: haemolysis (LDH >600, schistocytes), raised transaminases and platelets <100 × 10⁹/L.

Rapid progression: hepatic subcapsular haematoma + rupture, DIC + haemorrhage, AKI, pulmonary oedema, eclamptic seizure, abruption. Maternal mortality 1-3%, perinatal 10-30%.

Management is delivery at any gestation if maternal status deteriorating; steroids for fetal maturity if eligible and time permits; Mg for seizure prophylaxis even without prior eclampsia.

cards.front: Most malignancies of the vulva are [___] carcinomas.
cards.context:
Squamous carcinoma accounts for the great majority of vulval malignancies in both textbooks, whether the figure is put at ninety-five per cent or about ninety.

Melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and sarcoma are the remainder named beside that majority.

The malignant end of this range is therefore usually squamous, with a short list of rarer cancers beside it.

cards.front: Small for gestational age (SGA) = estimated fetal weight (EFW) <[___]; fetal growth restriction (FGR) is pathological, usually below the 3rd centile or abnormal Dopplers.
cards.context:
The trap: SGA is a size label, FGR is a diagnosis of failed growth potential.

SGA just means EFW <10th centile. Many are constitutionally small but healthy (small parents, female fetus), needing only surveillance to confirm normal velocity with normal Dopplers.

FGR means the fetus has not reached its growth potential: EFW or abdominal circumference <3rd centile, absent end-diastolic flow, or <10th with abnormal Dopplers or falling centiles. It can occur above the 10th.

cards.front: For a stable woman with hyperemesis and prolonged poor intake, the treating team gives IV [___] before a planned dextrose infusion to reduce Wernicke encephalopathy risk.
cards.context:
Prolonged poor intake in hyperemesis can deplete thiamine. NSW guidance advises supplementation before planned glucose-containing fluids and checking sodium first.

This is not a rule to delay emergency treatment of hypoglycaemia. Arrange prompt thiamine alongside urgent care; deficiency can cause serious neurological harm, but harm is not inevitable.

Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and other enzymes in glucose oxidation, so repletion before a glucose load reduces Wernicke risk.

cards.front: Neonatal iron stores increase when healthy term infants have cord clamping delayed at least [___].
cards.context: A delay of at least 60 seconds allows a placental-to-neonatal transfusion. That transfusion increases infant iron stores.

cards.front: For hysteroscopy in a healthy woman, the BSGE/ESGE maximum isotonic fluid deficit is [___] mL.
cards.context: BSGE/ESGE limits for healthy women are 1,000 mL hypotonic and 2,500 mL isotonic deficit. Agree lower limits for comorbidity with anaesthesia; these are society maxima, not a verified KEMH-specific threshold.
